analysis.one_liner: Requires companies to disclose their real human owners to states so police can trace shell companies.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to unmask anonymous shell companies was referred to the Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require anyone forming a corporation or limited liability company to tell the state the name, address, and ID number of each real owner — the 'beneficial owner' — and to keep that list updated. States would hold the records for five years and turn them over to police, prosecutors, courts, and federal investigators on request. The stated goal is to stop criminals, corrupt foreign officials, and tax evaders from hiding behind companies with no visible owner, a gap the bill says has been exploited by arms dealers and sanctions evaders. Today, a person can form a US company in under 24 hours online without naming a single real owner.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit indirectly: law enforcement gets a basic tool for tracing money laundering, health care and securities fraud, tax evasion, and sanctions evasion through US shell companies, which the bill says ultimately costs the public and funds crime. Honest small businesses also gain a more level field against fraudsters who currently use anonymous companies as vehicles for scams. Federal contractors would have to reveal their true owners when bidding on government work.

how_it_helps.text: Requires applicants for new corporations and LLCs in participating states to list each beneficial owner with name, street address, and a unique ID number from a passport or driver's license, and to update the list within 60 days of any change plus an annual filing [S3].

Requires states to keep ownership records for five years after a company terminates and to release them on subpoena, summons, or written request from federal agencies, foreign governments under treaties, or Treasury's FinCEN [S3].

Cites documented cases, including an arms dealer who used at least 12 companies incorporated in Texas, Florida, and Delaware, and Iranian interests that used a New York shell company to buy a Manhattan building and send rent money abroad until it was seized [S3].

Directs the Federal Acquisition Regulation to require contractors to submit beneficial ownership information with bids above the simplified acquisition threshold, so the government knows who it is buying from [S2].
Adds formation agents to the list of businesses that must run anti-money-laundering programs, with Treasury required to write the rule within 270 days [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The registered agent and company-formation industry would bear new duties: verifying identities, holding records, and running anti-money-laundering programs. States would need to build collection systems, though the bill authorizes up to $40 million from federal forfeiture funds to cover compliance costs. Small business owners would face filing paperwork and penalties of up to $1 million or three years in prison for false or missing filings, while larger companies with over 20 employees, banks, insurers, and most regulated entities are exempt.
analysis.who_pays_short: Formation agents, small businesses, and states

drawbacks.text: Compliance burdens fall on small businesses: the exemption list leaves out most regulated and large entities, so the disclosure duty lands mainly on small firms, which face civil penalties up to $1,000,000 and up to three years' imprisonment for false or incomplete filings [S3].

The bill imposes the requirement through Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant funding but expressly bars the Attorney General from withholding that funding from a noncomplying state, meaning the mandate has no real enforcement teeth against states [S3].

Collecting owner addresses and ID numbers in state databases creates a honeypot of sensitive personal data on millions of small business owners, and the bill leaves it to states to decide how much of it is publicly disclosed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — knowing who actually owns a company before law enforcement has to investigate it — is a modest, widely used safeguard: every EU country already requires formation agents to identify beneficial owners, while the US forms roughly two million companies a year with no owner information. The real weakness here is design, not principle: generous exemptions carve out large and regulated firms, and the funding lever cannot actually be pulled against a noncomplying state, so a determined state could opt out without consequence. The burden on honest small businesses is real but small, mostly paperwork.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and sent to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, joined by Senator Dianne Feinstein, introduced the bill on February 3, 2016, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S3][S5].
The bill attracted three cosponsors, two Democrats and one Republican [S4].
No further action was ever taken: the action history ends at the committee referral, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The company-formation and registered-agent industry, and anyone who relies on forming a US company without naming a real owner, were better off because the bill never advanced. States that market fast, anonymous incorporation kept their competitive edge, and law enforcement kept working without ownership records.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The registered agent and shell company industry

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — three cosponsors included a Republican — and no recorded vote or floor fight ever occurred, so no partisan pattern shows in the record.

industries.industry: Company formation and registered agent services
industries.note: The bill would make paid formation agents verify and hold beneficial owner information and run anti-money-laundering programs, directly raising the cost of their anonymity-selling service. Their interest in keeping incorporation anonymous runs against the public's interest in traceable companies.

industries.industry: States that sell incorporations (Delaware, Nevada, and others)
industries.note: States would have to collect and retain owner information for the roughly two million entities formed each year, undercutting the marketing pitch that a company can be formed online in 24 hours with no owner identified. Although the bill technically conditions compliance on federal grant money, it bars the Attorney General from actually withholding that funding, softening the blow.
Wealthy individuals, corrupt foreign officials, and criminal networks that use hidden-owner US companies for money laundering, sanctions evasion, and fraud would lose their anonymity channel.

Small owners would face new annual filings and penalties for wrong information, but they also gain when competitors can no longer hide behind faceless companies to run frauds. Large companies, banks, insurers, and other regulated firms are exempt.
Police and regulators get direct access to a registry of who owns each company, which the bill says is needed to investigate terrorism financing, drug trafficking, tax evasion, and corporate fraud.
